PullRequest.Title: Keep sandbox toggle editable when managed policy allows bypass
PullRequest.Body:
## Summary

Fixes #334265.

- Keep the standalone **Sandboxing for terminal** toggle editable when managed `sandbox.enabled` is `true` and `sandbox.allowBypass` is `true`, in both Editor chat and Sessions/Agents permissions pickers.
- Keep the toggle checked and disabled when managed sandboxing is enabled and bypass is false or unspecified; preserve existing behavior when managed sandboxing is not enabled.
- Distinguish required sandboxing from an editable managed default in the hover text and recheck policy in the toggle change handler.
- Watch `sandbox.allowBypass` through the native managed-settings pipeline and forward the new service dependency through the mobile picker.

### Scope

This change is limited to toggle editability. Existing checked-state logic and setting writes are preserved; it does not change SDK/runtime enforcement or add a trusted session-disable operation. The permissions picker itself and its permission-level choices are not disabled by this change.

## Validation

- `npm run typecheck-client` passed.
- 33 focused tests passed across the Editor picker, Sessions picker, and native managed-settings suites.
- Tests cover managed/unmanaged states, bypass true/false/unspecified, existing configured on/off values, and policy revalidation in an existing toggle callback.
- `npm run export-policy-data` completed successfully.
- No editor diagnostics; `git diff --check` passed.

Scenarios.Scenario: Open and use the Sessions/Agents desktop permission picker with the standalone sandbox toggle
Scenarios.CriticalPath: A user click synchronously builds a fixed-size permission list and the sandbox toggle before the action widget is shown. The diff adds one effective managed-setting lookup while constructing the toggle and one more lookup if the toggle changes; both are in-memory property reads and add no asynchronous work.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: The permission-level collection is small and fixed; added work does not scale with sessions, history, workspace size, or policy count.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Single UI-thread invocation per picker open or toggle action; no queue, parallelism, or new fan-out.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Resolved managed settings are already cached in AccountPolicyService._managedSettings. Cold and warm picker opens use the same O(1) object lookup; the picker does not initiate native reads or IPC.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the concrete getter implementation directly returns this._managedSettings[key], and the changed call is reached only while constructing or changing the toggle.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Exact picker-open frequency is user-dependent, but each invocation adds only a constant-time cached lookup.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression. The changed work is constant-time, synchronous, and negligible, with no added expensive boundary.

Scenarios.Scenario: Open/filter/use the Agent Host auto-approve picker and its sandbox toggle
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Opening awaits the existing item-resolution path, then constructs action items and the sandbox toggle. For dynamic schemas, filtering is already debounced by 200 ms and may await agent-host completions; the new policy lookup occurs only after that existing work and does not delay it materially.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Request dynamic session configuration completions from the agent host when enumDynamic is set.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most one completion request per 200 ms debounced filter result; static auto-approve schemas make zero calls.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same completion request and debounce behavior occurred before the diff.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: When applicable, the existing completion request must finish before filtered items are shown. The new managed-setting read happens afterward and does not alter request count or scheduling.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Filter keystrokes are coalesced at 200 ms; added cost remains one local lookup per resulting refresh rather than scaling with item count.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Filter requests are serialized/coalesced through the existing Delayer; the change adds no request or task and performs one cached lookup per delivered result. Toggle handling is a single synchronous lookup followed by the pre-existing configuration write.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The bypass policy value is read from the already-resolved in-memory settings bag on every construction. No new cache key, miss path, or invalidation behavior is introduced.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the call order and getter implementation show the diff adds only O(1) local work after existing item retrieval.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Dynamic auto-approve schemas may be uncommon, but that uncertainty does not affect the conclusion because their boundary behavior is unchanged.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression. Existing IPC cardinality, debounce, configuration writes, and rendering remain unchanged.

Scenarios.Scenario: Initialize native managed settings and react to runtime changes of sandbox.allowBypass
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Startup creates the existing native policy watcher and performs the existing one-time IPC initialization; adding the key enlarges the watcher definition and possible settings payload by one boolean. Runtime policy changes propagate through the existing event path. This is off picker-open and render critical paths.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Create one @vscode/policy-watcher native watcher over managed-policy definitions.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One watcher creation at initialization or definition-set replacement; the diff adds one key to the existing watcher, not another watcher.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same watcher was created for the existing control and policy keys; only the definition count increases by one.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Initial watcher callback must complete native managed-settings initialization, but the incremental payload is one boolean definition.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Fetch the initialized managed-settings object from the native service and receive subsequent change events.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One initialization call per client plus one event per actual native settings update; the diff does not add a channel or initialization call.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same single IPC call and shared event stream existed, with a payload lacking sandbox.allowBypass.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The initialization call is background-started by the client and serves all managed keys together.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: A runtime native-setting change can run the existing default-account refresh pipeline, whose entitlement and managed-settings fetches may issue authenticated HTTP requests when their freshness checks require it.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most one coalesced refresh per 100 ms burst; individual endpoint calls are conditional on authentication and existing freshness caches. The new key can now be one trigger when an administrator changes it.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Changes to sandbox.allowBypass were not watched and therefore could not trigger this refresh path; other native managed-setting changes already did.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Background policy/account refresh; it does not block opening or interacting with the picker.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Startup overhead grows by one definition and at most one boolean in the payload. Runtime work scales with actual administrator changes, coalesced per client rather than with picker usage or workspace size.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: One native watcher covers all definitions. Watcher replacement is serialized by Throttler; account refreshes caused by source changes are coalesced by a 100 ms ThrottledDelayer.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The watcher and IPC client retain a single current settings object. Effective values are recomputed only on actual changes. Account refresh endpoint work remains guarded by existing freshness caches, rate-limit backoff, and 100 ms coalescing.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High for the event and refresh call path; medium for actual HTTP execution because endpoint freshness and authentication can suppress requests.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Enterprise policy updates can reach many clients, but changes to this boolean are expected to be rare and cached endpoint checks may eliminate network I/O; the fixed one-key watcher overhead is negligible.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression. The only new boundary trigger is a rare, coalesced policy-change event; startup call counts are unchanged and the incremental data/work is bounded.

Scenarios.Scenario: Construct and use the mobile permission picker
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Dependency injection now forwards the existing managed-settings service to the base picker. Phone-layout sheet construction does not consult the new bypass value; desktop-layout fallback uses the same single cached lookup as the desktop picker.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Constant per picker instance/open; independent of session or item count.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Single picker instance and UI action; no added asynchronous work or concurrency.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No new cache behavior on phone layout. Desktop fallback reads the same resident effective-settings object.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High from the subclass implementation and base call path.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Viewport mix is irrelevant because neither path introduces an expensive operation.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression. Constructor forwarding itself performs no additional work, and the only reachable lookup is O(1).

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all seven changed files and all diff hunks. Traced picker rendering/input, native policy startup and updates, IPC propagation, caching, coalescing, and the transitive account-refresh network path. No high-confidence actionable performance regression was found.

Stats.CostNote: Copilot SDK reports nano-AI units and model billing multipliers; it does not provide a USD conversion.
